How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.
  • Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.
  • Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may not need to work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires. Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may not need to work. Indeed, studies show that employees at post-IPO companies are more likely to leave their jobs or become less satisfied. Management experts and executives who have successfully navigated IPOs say there are a few ways companies can make sure that doesn’t happen. GIVE EMPLOYEES A REASON TO WORK OTHER THAN MONEY The most key thing is to make sure workers have a sense of purpose that goes beyond making money—something Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin highlighted explicitly in a letter to prospective shareholders when the manufacturer went public in 2004. “Talented people are attracted to Google because we empower them to change the world,” they wrote. “We are focused on providing an environment where talented, hardworking people are rewarded for their contributions to Google and for making the world a better place.” Laszlo Bock, who oversaw Google’s human resources operations for a decade following its IPO, echoed that sentiment almost a decade later. “We spend more time working than we do on almost any other activity in our lives,” he wrote. “People want all that time to mean something.” Of course, it is ideal if that sense of purpose is already in place before a company goes public. “If a company’s employees are coming to work just to make money, it’s over,” venture capitalist Paul Koontz remarked in 2004. “There need to be some bigger ambitions, some more fundamental calling that motivates a company.” GIVE WOULD-BE ENTREPRENEURS FREEDOM TO EXPERIMENT One of the biggest risks for post-IPO companies is that their most talented and entrepreneurial employees now have the resources to launch their own ventures. In fact, the effect is so powerful that at least one study has identified a causal link between the rate of IPOs in the economy and the rate of upcoming firm creation. While it may be impossible to prevent these exits altogether, post-IPO companies should ensure that their most talented staff have the freedom and resources to pursue their own ideas. “There has to be safe space for entrepreneurial employees,” Syracuse University professor Carl Schramm said in 2018. “There has to be some space where people can actually try and push an idea around, scope it out, [and] have a friendly ear someplace in the hierarchy of the company.” Management should also consider giving top talent their own discretionary research budgets. In the mid-2010s, Adobe launched a program that gave its workers $1,000 to spend however they liked, with no explanation or justification required. “When you trust people, they’ll live up to your expectations,” Adobe Chief Strategist and Vice President of Creativity Mark Randall told Fast Company. “They’ll allocate their resources and figure out how to move ahead.” DON’T LET WEALTH CREATE A NEW OFFICE HIERARCHY IPOs can create an awkward social dynamic in which employees’ wealth bears little relationship to their seniority, or even their contributions to the company. This can leave managers supervising employees who have several times their network, and newcomers resenting colleagues who got rich doing the same basic job. Post-IPO companies should acknowledge this dynamic instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Ahead of Google’s IPO, clinical psychologist Steven Goldbart recommended that companies organize workshops for employees to discuss how their newfound wealth affects workplace relationships, job expectations, and corporate culture. “The biggest mistake a company can make is to pretend [an IPO] has no impact,” he said. Executive compensation consultants Todd Sirras and Austin Vanbastelaer also recommend giving managers more power to reward top performers, including by “increasing responsibilities, expanding strategic opportunities, and promoting visibility and engagement with senior executives.” PAY ATTENTION TO WELLBEING AND WORKING CONDITIONS Employees at startups often put up with grueling hours and difficult work conditions knowing they may be in line for a big payoff. Once the payoff arrives, however, their tolerance for those things may go away. And new stressors will also emerge, including increased bureaucracy, regulatory burdens, and the pressure to meet quarterly earnings. Indeed, one study that analyzed 3.7 million Glassdoor reviews found that employee ratings of senior management and work-life balance declined by 10% and 6.6% following IPOs. Post-IPO companies must keep their finger on the pulse of their workforce to identify any percolating dissent. For example, in the run-up to Google’s 2004 IPO, Silicon Valley executive coach Laura Steck advised companies preparing to go public to survey employees about how to improve working conditions. Management may also simply need to take their foot off the gas pedal a little bit. In one study, published earlier this year, researchers from the University of Alabama and the University of Iowa examined the management practices and long-term survival of 183 companies that went public in 1996. They found that companies are more likely to survive if executives strike the right balance between maintaining a sense of urgency and valuing employees. “Too little sense of urgency can lead to complacency while too much urgency can lead to burnout, lower quality output, and other undesirable consequences,” the authors wrote.

Recent findings suggest that IPOs can create an awkward social dynamic in which employees’ wealth bears little relationship to their seniority, or even their contributions to the firm. This can leave managers supervising employees who have several times their network, and newcomers resenting colleagues who got rich doing the same basic job.

Post-IPO companies should acknowledge this dynamic instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Ahead of Google’s IPO, clinical psychologist Steven Goldbart recommended that companies organize workshops for employees to discuss how their newfound wealth affects workplace relationships, job expectations, and corporate culture.

“The biggest mistake a firm can make is to pretend [an IPO] has no impact,” he stated.

Executive compensation consultants Todd Sirras and Austin Vanbastelaer also recommend giving managers more power to reward top performers, including by “increasing responsibilities, expanding strategic opportunities, and promoting visibility and engagement with senior executives.”.

According to recent reports, employees at startups often put up with grueling hours and difficult work conditions knowing they may be in line for a big payoff. Once the payoff arrives, however, their tolerance for those things may go away.

Industry observers note that and new stressors will also emerge, including increased bureaucracy, regulatory burdens, and the pressure to meet quarterly earnings. Indeed, one study that analyzed 3.7 million Glassdoor reviews found that employee ratings of senior management and work-life balance declined by 10% and 6.6% following IPOs.

Industry observers note that post-IPO companies must keep their finger on the pulse of their workforce to identify any percolating dissent. For example, in the run-up to Google’s 2004 IPO, Silicon Valley executive coach Laura Steck advised companies preparing to go public to survey employees about how to improve working conditions.

Management may also simply need to take their foot off the gas pedal a little bit. In one study, published earlier this year, researchers from the University of Alabama and the University of Iowa examined the management practices and long-term survival of 183 companies that went public in 1996.

They found that companies are more likely to survive if executives strike the right balance between maintaining a sense of urgency and valuing employees.

“Too little sense of urgency can lead to complacency while too much urgency can lead to burnout, lower quality output, and other undesirable consequences,” the authors wrote.

I recently met a venture fund founder in the sauna at the Ritz-Carlton in Dallas. We spent about 10 minutes together and got deep into science and tech in the wellness world. We also spoke about taking care of our aging parents. We got further in those 10 minutes than most people do in months of coffee meetings, and we’ve stayed in touch ever since.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t play golf, but I know plenty of business still gets done on the course. For me, the most honest business and personal conversations happen half-naked, sweating and uncomfortable. It’s the truth, literally.

In 2023, I wrote here that a sauna session could leave you primed to negotiate or close a deal. I’ve since changed my mind about the order of operations. The sauna doesn’t help you close. It helps you trust, and the deals follow.

Recent findings suggest that CNN recently named a sauna as Barcelona’s hottest new nightlife spot, with a spa turning into a rave for 100 people built around wellness and sobriety. London’s ARC opened with a 65-person sauna and DJ sets. In New York, The Altar planned a 50-person sauna on Fifth Avenue.

Clubs aren’t disappearing, but the job they did for us, getting adults to drop their guard together, now has a newly introduced home. Only 54% of U.S. adults say they drink, matching the lowest level Gallup has recorded since 1939. I’ve written about what that means for beverage founders and why recovery has become a KPI. What interests me now is what happens inside the room.

There’s a reason for what Gabby Reece called “the truth barrel,” the name of an older podcast she recorded in a sauna. It’s hard to perform when you’re half-dressed and dripping. There are no phones and nothing to hide behind. Everyone in the room is equally uncomfortable, and nobody’s title matters much after five minutes.

Sources indicate that when I sat in the most spacious sauna I’ve ever seen, at Love.Life in Los Angeles, the benches were full of pro athletes, coaches, trainers and founders comparing notes on our days and how we try to balance it all. More recently, I spent time in a 175-degree sauna at The Assembly Retreat, getting to know familiar faces and newly introduced connections alike. I’m a member of The Assembly, a network of investors, founders and operators in health and wellness, and those were some of the most intimate business and personal conversations I’ve had. No selling, no suits — except bathing suits. People help each other and tell the truth, and deal flow follows because you want to work with people you trust.

Industry observers note that the research points the same way. A 2026 paper covering 1,907 sauna users in the U.K. tied weekly sauna use to better self-reported physical and mental health, and belonging explained part of that link. The authors also linked ritual and shared emotion to stronger bonds. It’s self-reported data from people already into sauna culture, but it matches what I’ve experienced.

I’ve learned that trust rarely gets built across a table. Sit somewhere hot with someone, or sweat with them, and don’t sell them anything.

It has been revealed that the science is part of why I love the sauna and make it part of my routine three to four times a week. In a Finnish study of 2,315 men followed for about 20 years, those using a sauna four to seven times a week had a 50% lower risk of fatal cardiovascular disease than once-a-week people. A later study of 1,688 adults, about half of them women, found that the most frequent users had roughly a quarter of the rate of fatal cardiovascular events seen in once-weekly users. It’s not proof, but it’s enough to keep me on the bench.

In a recent development, it can also help you get more out of your workout. In an eight-week randomized trial of 47 inactive adults, adding a 15-minute sauna after exercise improved fitness, systolic blood pressure and total cholesterol more than exercise alone. Blood pressure fell an additional 8 mmHg. Exercise physiologist Dr. Stacy Sims writes about why heat training matters for women in particular.

According to recent reports, for mental health, the evidence is still early but promising. A small sham-controlled trial found that whole-body heat held promise for depression, though it used a medical heating setup, not a sauna. I don’t treat it as a cure. As I’ve written before, wellness shouldn’t feel like a second job. I keep the sauna because it’s one of the few health habits that also gives me time with people.

In a recent development, I prefer a traditional barrel sauna over infrared. Infrared warms up faster, but sessions run longer, and the long-term mortality research centers on traditional saunas. Saunas have been around for thousands of years, and I like that this one still works much the way it always has.

I keep mine at about 175°F and stay for 20 minutes. The workout trial above used about 175 to 179°F, and the Finnish data favored sessions longer than 19 minutes. If you’re new, start shorter and build up. Most notable, listen to your body.

Wear a hat to keep your head cooler so you can stay longer, and stick with natural fibers. The truest way to sauna is “no textiles,” but that’s tough to pull off with other people. Drink water, skip alcohol and cool down at your own pace. Check with your doctor first if you have a heart condition or any other health concern.

Studios are spreading too, including SweatHouz, with more than 100 locations, though its private suites, each with its own infrared sauna and cold plunge, are built for privacy more than community. If you are considering purchasing a sauna for your home, SISU is known for design and function, and we have a Redwood Outdoors barrel.

The conversation that matters most to me happens in my own backyard. My husband and I have about two sauna dates a week. Along with our non-negotiable long walk on Sundays, it’s where we connect and catch up.

Industry News: Struggling to Get Business Referrals? Here’s the Hurdle You May Not Realize You’re Creating.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I attend my share of networking events, and there’s one question I hear almost every time: “Who would be a good referral for you?”.
  • According to recent reports, it’s a fair question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I attend my share of networking events, and there’s one question I hear almost every time: “Who would be a good referral for you?”.

According to recent reports, it’s a fair question. But the answers usually sound something like this: business owners, CEOs, companies looking to grow or anyone who needs marketing.

I understand the instinct. Nobody wants to limit their opportunities. But think about the person listening. They might know hundreds of business owners. How are they supposed to recognize which one actually needs your help?

Recent findings suggest that I’ve learned that people don’t necessarily need more reminders to refer you. They need a clearer reason to think of you in the first place.

And there’s something else entrepreneurs often overlook. When someone makes an introduction, they’re not just sharing a contact. They’re putting their own reputation behind that recommendation.

According to recent reports, let’s say you’ve known someone professionally for several years. You enjoy their firm, respect their work and would happily meet them for coffee. Does that automatically mean you’d recommend them to an important client? Probably not.

You would want to know whether they could deliver, how they treated customers and whether making the introduction might put an existing relationship at risk. Your professional network makes those same judgments about you.

Sources indicate that this is why I don’t believe referrals should be treated as a numbers game. Having 500 contacts doesn’t mean you have 500 people willing to recommend your business. A smaller network of people who understand your expertise and trust how you operate may be far more valuable.

The real question isn’t how many people know you. It’s how many would feel comfortable putting their credibility behind you.

One mistake I see entrepreneurs make is describing their businesses too broadly.

“We provide strategic solutions.”.

“We offer comprehensive consulting services.”.

Recent findings suggest that these statements might be accurate, but they’re difficult for someone else to use. A better approach is to explain the situation that typically brings a customer to you.

For example, a business owner might say, “We work with companies that are generating plenty of leads but struggling to turn those inquiries into customers.”.

Sources indicate that now the person listening has something specific to recognize. They may remember a conversation with a founder complaining about poor conversion or a colleague frustrated with marketing spending that isn’t producing results.

Industry observers note that you haven’t asked them to memorize your service offerings. You’ve helped them identify a problem.

I made a related argument in my Entrepreneur article about businesses spending more on marketing while attracting fewer customers. Businesses can create plenty of activity without attracting the right opportunities.

According to recent reports, the same is true of networking. More introductions aren’t necessarily better if the people being introduced don’t need what you provide.

I’ve come to think of referrals as an extension of relationship marketing, where familiarity, credibility and genuine understanding matter more than the number of people reached. That distinction is explored in this discussion of relationship marketing for service-based businesses.

The underlying idea is straightforward: Someone needs a reason to trust your judgment before they’re comfortable sharing that trust with another person.

It has been revealed that for entrepreneurs, that confidence is built through ordinary professional behavior. Do you follow through when you promise something? Are you transparent about what you can and cannot deliver? Do you treat smaller opportunities with the same care as larger ones?

And when someone introduces a potential customer, do you take the time to understand their needs, or do you immediately launch into a sales pitch?

Sources indicate that people remember those experiences. They also remember when an introduction leaves them embarrassed.

If you want more referrals, protecting the confidence of the person making the introduction should be as important as winning the potential customer.

Here’s another question worth asking: Have you made it easy for someone to explain why your business is different?

Sources indicate that too often, entrepreneurs hand people a website or a long presentation and expect them to figure it out. I would rather give someone one useful observation they can remember and repeat.

It has been revealed that suppose you’re an accountant who helps growing businesses understand why profitability is declining despite increasing sales. You might explain that many companies focus on revenue without examining what each additional sale actually contributes to profit. That’s a conversation starter.

Someone who hears a business owner discussing shrinking margins can recognize the connection without having to understand every service you offer.

Being visible and being selected are different challenges. Referrals bring that distinction into focus. Someone can know your business exists without understanding why they should recommend it. Your responsibility is to close that gap.

There is something uncomfortable about networking relationships that feel entirely transactional.

You introduce someone to a prospective customer and immediately wonder when they’ll return the favor. You send a helpful article and expect a sales opportunity. You attend an event and measure success by the number of business cards collected.

In a recent development, I’ve never believed strong professional relationships work particularly well that way. Some connections lead to business swiftly. Others develop over years. Many never result in a transaction, and that’s perfectly fine.

I prefer to focus on whether I can make a useful connection, share something relevant or help someone think differently about a challenge.

That doesn’t mean abandoning commercial discipline. Keep track of conversations. Follow up when you’ve promised to. Understand which relationships are relevant to your business.

But don’t confuse relationship management with treating every interaction as a potential invoice. People can tell the difference.

According to recent reports, instead of introducing yourself by listing your services, describe one situation in which your business genuinely makes a difference. Keep it specific enough that someone could recognize it in a conversation with a friend or colleague.

Industry observers note that then ask three people you trust to explain what they think your business does. Don’t help them answer. Listen to the language they use and the problems they associate with you. If their answers are vague or completely different, that’s useful information. Your positioning may be less clear than you think.

It has been revealed that next, consider what happens after someone makes an introduction. Do you respond promptly? Do you acknowledge the person who connected you? Do you handle the conversation in a way that reinforces their confidence?

These small details determine whether someone will feel comfortable recommending you again.

Entrepreneurs spend considerable time trying to become more visible. We invest in marketing, attend events, publish content and build professional networks. Those efforts matter. But there’s a difference between being known and being recommended.

It has been revealed that you can’t demand someone’s trust, and you can’t manufacture a meaningful referral through repeated requests. You can, however, make your expertise easier to understand, consistently deliver on your commitments and treat every introduction with care.

Before your next networking event, I’d encourage you to stop asking how many people you can meet. Ask yourself something more useful: If someone recommended me to a person they deeply respect, would I make them glad they did?

That’s the standard worth building a business around.

It’s a fair question. But the answers usually sound something like this: business owners, CEOs, companies looking to grow or anyone who needs marketing.

Transactional emails are easy to overlook during application development. A registration form works, the database stores the user's information, and the backend successfully triggers an email. Everything appears to be functioning as expected.

Then a user reports that their password-reset message never arrived.

The problem might not be in the email template or the sending function. It could involve DNS configuration, authentication failures, message formatting, queue processing, recipient-server policies, or an incorrectly configured production environment.

It has been revealed that for developers building SaaS applications, ecommerce platforms, and web services, reliable email delivery is an important part of the user experience. An account-verification message that never arrives can prevent someone from accessing an application, while a delayed security notification can create unnecessary confusion.

Understanding how to investigate these problems requires looking beyond the email-sending function. This guide explores a practical debugging workflow, the technical layers involved, and the tools developers can use to identify common email delivery failures.

One of the first mistakes developers make when troubleshooting email is assuming that a successful API response means the message has reached the recipient.

These are two different events.

When an application submits an email through an SMTP server or an email service provider's API, the provider may accept the request and return a successful response. However, the receiving mail server still needs to process the message.

Depending on its configuration and policies, the receiving server might:.

Accept the message and place it in the inbox.

Accept the message but classify it as spam.

Reject the message because of authentication or policy challenges.

Accept the message but place it in another folder.

A successful request therefore confirms only that a particular stage of the process completed.

Developers should distinguish between three notable states:.

Submission: The application successfully handed the message to its sending provider.

Acceptance: The receiving mail server accepted responsibility for the message.

Inbox placement: The message became visible in the recipient's expected inbox.

These distinctions make troubleshooting considerably easier. Instead of immediately rewriting an email template, developers can identify which stage is actually failing.

Before investigating external email infrastructure, examine the application's own implementation.

Sources indicate that A common example is a password-reset workflow. The application receives a request, generates a temporary token, creates a reset URL, and sends an email containing that URL.

Several problems can occur before the message even reaches an email provider.

The application generates an expired token.

The reset URL points to a staging environment.

An asynchronous task fails before processing the message.

The email service credentials are incorrect.

An API request times out without being retried.

The application records success before confirming the provider's response.

Start by logging the key stages of the process.

For example, a Node.js application might use structured logging:.

This example assumes that the email provider returns a message identifier. Adapt the response fields to the actual SDK being used.

Notice that the logs identify the recipient through an internal ID rather than exposing their complete email address.

Avoid logging passwords, authentication tokens, reset URLs, or other sensitive information.

The objective is to establish a traceable record of what happened without introducing additional security risks.

Email authentication is another notable area to investigate when messages are rejected or consistently classified as spam.

Three commonly used mechanisms help receiving servers evaluate whether a message is authorized to represent a particular domain.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allows a domain owner to specify which servers are authorized to send messages using that domain.

This information is published through DNS.

A simplified SPF record might look like this:.

The actual record must reflect the sending services authorized by the domain owner.

Common configuration mistakes include:.

Forgetting to authorize a new email provider.

Publishing multiple SPF records for the same domain.

Exceeding SPF's DNS lookup limit.

Leaving outdated sending services in the record.

In a recent development, remember that SPF evaluates the sending infrastructure against the envelope sender domain. It does not automatically guarantee that the visible From address is aligned.

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages.

The receiving server can retrieve the corresponding public key through DNS and verify that the signature is valid.

A failed DKIM check might indicate:.

A mismatch between the configured selector and published record.

Message modification after signing.

Developers integrating multiple email providers should verify that each provider has the correct signing configuration.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) builds on SPF and DKIM.

It allows domain owners to define how receiving servers should handle messages that fail authentication and alignment requirements.

A basic monitoring-oriented DMARC record might look like this:.

This is an illustrative configuration. The reporting address must be valid, and the domain should have an appropriate monitoring and policy-enforcement plan.

Developers can use MXToolbox to inspect DNS records and investigate common authentication problems.

For additional technical background, SitePoint's guide to HTML email development explains why email environments require different implementation considerations from ordinary web pages.

An email template that looks perfect in a browser can behave differently when rendered by Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, or another email client.

This happens because email clients do not implement HTML and CSS in exactly the same way.

A layout may break because of unsupported CSS properties, image restrictions, unexpected font rendering, or differences in how tables are handled.

For this reason, email testing should be part of the development process rather than something performed only after owners report a problem.

A useful testing sequence includes:.

HTML validation: Check the markup for malformed elements, missing attributes, and unnecessary code.

Rendering tests: Preview the email across desktop and mobile email clients.

Link verification: Confirm that buttons, links, and personalized URLs point to the correct destinations.

Image testing: Check whether the message remains understandable when images are blocked.

Content inspection: Review subject lines, sender information, and the plain-text alternative.

Deliverability checks: Examine authentication, content-related warnings, and potential inbox placement problems.

Developers can also incorporate pre-send diagnostics into their release workflow to identify potential deliverability problems before a message is sent to a larger audience.

The important point is to treat these checks as one part of quality assurance, not as a guarantee that every message will reach the primary inbox.

For more information about email rendering differences, SitePoint's article on essential HTML email coding tips provides useful examples of client-specific behavior.

Testing transactional emails with real customer addresses during development can create unnecessary problems.

A better approach is to use a dedicated testing environment that captures outgoing messages without delivering them to actual recipients.

For example, Mailpit provides a local SMTP server and web interface for inspecting messages during development.

It allows developers to examine:.

Email subject lines and headers.

Embedded images and attachments.

The final output generated by the application.

Another option is Mailtrap, which provides email testing capabilities for development workflows.

Consider a registration feature that sends a welcome message whenever a latest user creates an account.

Instead of sending hundreds of test messages to real addresses, developers can configure the development environment to capture them in a testing inbox.

This makes it possible to repeatedly test different templates without affecting actual customers or generating unnecessary email traffic.

A separate testing environment also reduces the risk of accidentally sending development notifications to production consumers.

Applications that send large numbers of emails often use background workers instead of processing every message during the original HTTP request.

This approach helps keep the application responsive, but it introduces another potential source of failures.

Imagine an ecommerce application that sends order confirmations after checkout.

Recent findings suggest that the application creates an order successfully and places an email task in a queue. However, the background worker becomes unavailable before processing the task.

The customer receives an order confirmation much later than expected, or perhaps not at all.

To investigate these problems, developers should monitor:.

Retries are particularly vital, but they need to be implemented carefully.

A temporary network failure may justify another attempt. A permanent rejection caused by an invalid recipient address usually does not.

Exponential backoff can help prevent repeated requests from overwhelming an unavailable service.

In a production system, add random jitter to avoid having multiple workers retry simultaneously.

In a recent development, also consider idempotency. If a worker processes the same task twice, the application should avoid sending duplicate transactional messages whenever possible.

A reliable queue architecture should distinguish between temporary failures and permanent failures rather than retrying every error indefinitely.

Testing before deployment is vital, but it cannot reveal every issue that may occur in production.

Real email traffic introduces changing conditions, including recipient-server behavior, sender reputation, invalid addresses, and differences between email providers.

Developers should therefore establish ongoing monitoring.

For Gmail-related monitoring, Google Postmaster Tools provides information about domain reputation, spam rates, and authentication.

It is particularly useful for teams sending enough email to generate meaningful reporting data.

Another useful resource is Can I Email, which documents HTML and CSS feature support across email clients.

According to recent reports, these tools address different problems. Monitoring sender reputation will not fix a broken password-reset URL, just as validating HTML will not resolve a DNS authentication failure.

The best approach is to monitor each layer independently.

A repeatable checklist helps developers investigate problems without overlooking notable details.

Before releasing a latest email feature, review the following:.

Confirm that the application successfully submits the message.

Verify that provider credentials and environment variables are correct.

Check the SMTP or API response.

Inspect SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration.

Validate the HTML and plain-text versions.

Test links and personalized content.

Preview the message on desktop and mobile email clients.

Verify that development and production configurations are separated.

Test queue failures and retry behavior.

Check delivery events and provider error reports.

Monitor bounce and complaint rates after deployment.

Not every application needs an expensive testing platform or a complicated monitoring stack.

A small project might only require a local email testing environment, basic DNS checks, and structured application logs.

A larger SaaS platform may benefit from automated integration tests, provider webhooks, queue monitoring, authentication reports, and dedicated deliverability testing.

The right setup depends on the application's sending volume, complexity, and the importance of its email workflows.

Reliable email delivery requires more than calling an SMTP function or integrating an email API.

Developers need to understand the complete process, from application logic and message construction to authentication, queue processing, recipient-server acceptance, and inbox placement.

The most effective troubleshooting strategy is to isolate these layers instead of treating every missing message as a template problem.

Start with application logs, inspect provider responses, validate authentication records, test email rendering, and monitor production behavior.

By incorporating these checks into development and deployment workflows, teams can reduce avoidable failures and build applications that communicate more reliably with their users.

TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

Sources indicate that transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model. Since then, we've continuously aimed to add state-of-the-art architectures, initially focused on NLP, then growing to Audio and computer vision. Today, transformers is the default library for LLMs and VLMs in the Python ecosystem.

In a recent development, transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 newly introduced architectures added every week. We have aimed for these architectures to be released in a timely manner; having day-0 support for the most sought-after architectures (Llamas, Qwens, GLMs, etc.).

Over time, Transformers has become a central component in the ML ecosystem, becoming one of the most complete toolkits in terms of model diversity; it's integrated in all popular training frameworks such as Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, TRL, Nanotron, etc.

Recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, ...) for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

As an example, here is how you would work with the transformers backend in vLLM:.

That's all it takes for a fresh model to enjoy super-fast and production-grade serving with vLLM!

Read more about it in the vLLM documentation.

According to recent reports, we've also been working very closely with llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

We are super proud that the transformers format is being adopted by the community, bringing a lot of interoperability we all benefit from. Train a model with Unsloth, deploy it with SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp to run locally! We aim to keep supporting the community going forward.

To make it easier for the community to use transformers as a reference for model definitions, we strive to significantly reduce the barrier to model contributions. We have been doing this effort for a few years, but we'll accelerate significantly over the next few weeks:.

As a model user, in the future you should see even more interoperability in the tools that you use.

This does not mean that we intend to lock you in using transformers in your experiments; rather, it means that thanks to this modeling standardization, you can expect the tools that you use for training, for inference, and for production, to efficiently work together.

As a model creator, this means that a single contribution will get your model available in all downstream libraries that have integrated that modeling implementation. We have seen this many times over the years: releasing a model is stressful and integrating in all key libraries is often a significant time-sink.

By standardizing the model implementation in a community-driven manner, we hope to lower the barrier of contributions to the field across libraries.

It has been revealed that we firmly believe this renewed direction will help standardize an ecosystem which is often at risk of fragmentation. We'd love to hear your feedback on the direction the team has decided to take; and of changes we could do to get there. Please come and see us over at the transformers-community support tab on the Hub!

Sources indicate that awesome news! Transformers being the default access point for as many models on day 0 as well as in being able to use the inference engine of choice is an epic goal!

if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

It's interesting, but it seems regardless of the TLDR, Llama.CPP maintains its own implementation and so won't benefit from any "day-0 support" for new architectures in Transfomers. I was kind of hoping Llama would get straight Transformer compatibility for a moment.

It's not clear what, if anything, is changing there.

You're entirely correct that llama.cpp maintains its own implementation; we've been working hand-in-hand with the team to get better intercompatibility however: export between frameworks on both sides (from transformers to llama.cpp, and vice-versa).

Additionally, with the frequent VLM releases happening recently, we've been working directly with @ngxson to have the implementations day-0 (or week-0) in llama.cpp when the implementation already exists in transformers.

We won't have "automatic day-0 support" as the two libs have different backends; but we can still try by making the two more compatible, reducing the time needed to get there.

Sources indicate that thanks @lysandre . Apologies if I sounded overly negative at all, it's a very good goal.

Since I doubt Llama.cpp would implement Transformers directly as VLM did (although that would be nice), perhaps an in-between project is possible using the low-level C bindings Llama provides. I believe that's how llama-cpp-python and similar work.

Then again I'm not sure how much benefit there is, but food for thought.

Breaking: Xreal Aura Review: Android XR combined with lightweight glasses delivers a true next-gen spatial computing experience

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you can get past the $1,000+ price of entry, the Xreal Aura really ups the ante for low-impact spatial computing.
  • Powerful Computing Puck adds another form of input.
  • Familiar Android XR interface+ Access to the vast Android ecosystem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you can get past the $1,000+ price of entry, the Xreal Aura really ups the ante for low-impact spatial computing.

Powerful Computing Puck adds another form of input.

Familiar Android XR interface+ Access to the vast Android ecosystem.

Can be used with Macs, Windows, and SteamOS devices.

$1,099 starting price might scare off potential customers.

Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In a recent development, the world of augmented reality (AR) and extended reality (XR) glasses is really starting to get interesting. This is particularly true of so-called “self-contained” systems that don’t rely solely on your smartphone or tablet to deliver content. The Xreal Aura, which was co-developed with Google, is the latest in the Android XR field, and it’s quite an ambitious project.

It has been revealed that although the Aura looks somewhat similar to previous Xreal glasses that we’ve reviewed, the AR goes a step further with a dedicated puck powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite SoC, hand/finger tracking, and the ability to interface wirelessly with accessories like keyboards and gamepads. The Aura really promises the ability to leave your smartphone at home and serve as the only computing platform you need (with some caveats).

The Aura’s design is clearly an evolution of the Xreal One Series, but with a few key differences. You’ll find the main changes up front, where you’ll now find two forward-facing, high-precision tracking cameras mounted at the corners of the frame. These cameras are used to continually track your head position, giving you the best possible experience for 6 degrees of freedom tracking for your hands and fingers.

At the center of the frame, there is a fully integrated single high-resolution camera for capturing photos or video. This was previously a separate add-on module for Xreal One Series AR glasses. There’s a red LED that illuminates when you’re recording so that people around you are made well aware of what’s going on if they have objections.

Industry observers note that your primary focal point, however, will be looking through the lenses, which are augmented by dual Sony-manufactured micro-OLED displays. You get one micro-OLED display per eye, each offering 1920 x 1200 resolution, a 120 Hz refresh rate, and maximum brightness of 1,050 nits. However, there’s a major upgrade in the field of view (FoV), as the Aura expands to 70 degrees, up from 57 degrees on the One Pro.

Industry observers note that the Aura is available in two SKUs to support the interpupillary distance (IPD) of a wide range of people. The Medium SKU supports people with an IPD of 60 to 66 mm, while the Large SKU ranges from 66 mm to 72 mm.

Given that the Aura is the flagship of Xreal’s AR/XR glasses lineup, it comes with electrochromic dimming for the lenses, which can automatically adjust transparency levels, or you can manually make adjustments (there are five levels of transparency available).

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The arms of the Aura look nearly identical to the ones you find on members of the One Series glasses. On the bottom is a red button, which, when pressed, allows you to manually adjust the brightness levels of the Aura. Directly adjacent is a rocker that allows you to control the volume. There’s another button on the top of the right arm that, when pressed once, takes you to the home menu. Double-pressing the button brings up the capture menu for taking pictures or videos with the forward-facing camera.

Bose-tuned speakers are also built into the arms of the Aura and feature an open-ear design so that you can remain engaged with what’s happening in your environment.

USB-C, Bluetooth 5.3, Wi-Fi 6E, GPS.

Industry observers note that xreal takes a two-pronged approach to hardware with the Aura. At a base level, the Aura is powered by the X1S Spatial Coprocessor, which allows you to experience traditional AR functionality with smartphones, tablets, PCs, and Macs, as you would with previous Xreal glasses.

But the real magic happens with the Xreal Computing Puck, which is a separate device that connects to the Aura using a USB-C cable. The puck looks and feels like a slightly oversized smartphone, albeit without a display. In place of the display, you’ll find a large touch-sensitive surface that can be used to interface with the Android XR interface.

Recent findings suggest that the puck is powered by Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform, which delivers 48 TOPS of AI computing power. It comes in 12GB RAM/256GB storage or 16GB RAM/512GB SKUs — our review unit was spec’d with the former. The puck features a 4,455 mAh battery that powers the glasses, and it even incorporates a fingerprint reader for authentication purposes in Android XR. The puck also fully supports Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3; the latter of which is essential for supporting Bluetooth accessories.

In a recent development, the puck is quite beefy, measuring roughly 5.85 x 2.85 x 0.5 inches and weighing 9.3 ounces. I had no concern just slipping the puck into my pants pocket, but Xreal also includes a detachable clip if you want to attach it to your pants pocket or other clothing. The puck also features a cooling fan to keep temperatures in check. Indeed, the device can get warm to the touch (after all, it’s basically a powerful screenless smartphone with a 4,455 mAh battery) during use – which explains why Xreal includes the clip and probably doesn’t want you putting the puck in your pocket, like I was prone to do.

My Aura review unit also came with an Xreal Keyboard and an Xreal Game Controller. Both connect to the Aura using Bluetooth and were easily set up by pairing them within the Bluetooth menu under Settings.

Industry observers note that the keyboard is battery-powered and is recharged using a USB-C port at the top (just above the F7 key). It’s a nifty design that neatly folds when not in use. Interestingly, I couldn’t find a way to “lock” the hinged part of the keyboard when it’s fully extended. Because of this, you can’t use the keyboard sitting on your lap with your legs spread slightly apart, as the keyboard will simply collapse and fall to the floor if you apply any kind of pressure. You’ll either need to put your legs together or place the keyboard on a desk or table, which isn’t exactly ideal if you like the more “freeing” aspect of using XR glasses.

With that said, the keyboard is a lifesaver when it comes to text entry, be it for entering web addresses, writing emails, or anything that requires frequent use of the keyboard. It sure beats waving your fingers around to input text.

Sources indicate that the game controller features an Xbox-style layout with four face buttons for gaming, two thumbsticks, a D-pad, and a Google Gemini/Home button. There are two shoulder buttons at the top and two triggers (with modes to function as microswitch triggers or Hall Effect analog triggers). There are also two remappable macro buttons under the shoulder buttons and two additional macro buttons on the underside of the controller (which can be turned off with physical switches).

Not only does the controller feature built-in rumble, but it also incorporates a 6-axis gyroscope for aiming and finger controls and a 3.5mm headphone jack built into the bottom of the unit. But perhaps the most interesting feature is a magnetic faceplate that breaks into three pieces. The main piece covers the face buttons, D-pad, and thumbsticks. The other two pieces cover the hand grips. You can purchase separate pieces to customize the look of the controller if you wish.

I found the controller comfortable to use, with a nice textured plastic finish for your palms to rest on (the bottom of the controller features a similar texture, but has a rubber coating over the plastic for better grip). And although the controller is designed for Bluetooth use with the Aura, it does feature a USB-C port and a USB dongle for connecting it wirelessly to a PC.

Recent findings suggest that another nice touch is that Xreal includes a charging dock for the controller that plugs in with a lengthy USB-A to USB-C cable. The controller itself charges with four pogo pins mounted on top of the dock (or via USB-C if you prefer).

After removing the Aura from its retail box, I wanted to get into the action quickly and didn’t bother initially charging the puck. I used the included USB-C to USB-C cable to plug from the left arm of the Aura into the dedicated USB-C port on the bottom of the puck. Next, I pressed the power button on the puck, after which the glasses sprang to life and began the setup process.

In a recent development, after taking some time to get used to dragging and pinching through the Android XR interface using my fingers, the experience began to feel almost natural. I was able to pinch to open apps, have multiple apps open at once, and drag or resize windows in my viewing space on command.

Recent findings suggest that I was able to access all the typical stock apps like Chrome, Gmail, and Google Photos, which, of course, carried over my favorites, emails, and photos/vidoes, respectively. I spent quite a bit of time going down memory lane, watching videos of my two sons when they were toddlers among the hundreds of videos I have stored in Google Photos. It was also great to be navigating around the UI or working in the app, then seeing a notification pop up telling me that an email had arrived. I would then pinch the notification with my fingers to open Gmail.

It has been revealed that the possibilities of how you can use the Aura are almost endless, and you can even mix other computing devices into the formula. For example, I was able to plug a USB-C cable from my MacBook Air into the second USB-C port on the puck (that’s usually reserved for recharging the puck). In an instant, my MacBook Air’s display was mirrored onto the glasses in front of me. So I could have Google Docs open as I typed, while having the Android XR native Gmail and YouTube apps flanking the virtual MacBook Air display.

It’s a similar experience with handheld gaming consoles. I was successfully able to connect a Lenovo Legion Go S (SteamOS) and an MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Windows 11) to the Aura glasses without problem, enjoying a vast library of games in fully immersive glory.

According to recent reports, the native gaming experience isn’t bad either; I loaded up games like Fortnite and spent an hour toiling around in Grand Theft Auto III for a nostalgic treat ahead of the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. The Xreal Game Controller made playing these games a breeze.

Industry observers note that but I also used the Aura glasses for more mundane tasks. I was able to walk around the house, performing my usual chores, with a shrunken YouTube window playing videos in the top right corner of my field of view. True multitasking is at hand, folks.

Industry observers note that I should note that open-air speakers sounded good, but not great. They sounded similar to the Bose-tuned speakers in the older Xreal One Pro. There's a good level of bass, and overall clarity is good. However, if you want a more immersive audio experience, the design of the Aura allows you to easily throw on a pair of headphones or wireless earbuds to compensate for any audio shortcomings.

According to recent reports, the Xrea Aura is a true workhorse when it comes to spatial computing. By putting the bulk of the computing hardware into a smartphone-shaped Computing Puck, you have a low-impact way of experiencing XR without the hassle of wearing a bulky headset.

It has been revealed that you can navigate the user interface using your hands, or the touch service of the puck. And for more specialized tasks, Xreal offers its own-branded keyboard and gamepad accessories (although you are free to use your own Bluetooth-enabled accessories).

Not only do you have access to the vast Android app ecosystem, but you can also connect to devices running Windows, macOS, or even SteamOS.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a lot going on with this device, and there are limitless possibilities for how you could use the Aura. The only problem is that most people don’t have limitless funds, so the $1,099 price tag of our review unit (12GB RAM, 256GB of storage) is sure to give many people pause. Stepping up to 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage takes the price to $1,299. If you add in the Xreal Keyboard and Xreal Game Controller, the total cost of our review unit comes in at $1,277 ($1,477 for the 16GB/512GB configuration).

That’s a lot to ask for what is essentially a niche device. However, if you want a truly immersive XR experience that is not weighed down by geeky-looking headsets, it’s hard to argue with what Xreal is offering with the Aura.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this blogpost, we present the key highlights and rationales about the Falcon-Edge series - a collection of powerful, universal, and fine-tunable language models available in ternary format, based on the BitNet architecture.

In a recent development, drawing from our experience with BitNet, Falcon-Edge introduces and validates an newly introduced pre-training paradigm that delivers a full-scope output from a single training process, simultaneously yielding both non-quantized and quantized model variants. This comprehensive approach produces a non-BitNet model in bfloat16 format, the native BitNet model, and a pre-quantized BitNet variant specifically engineered for effortless fine-tuning, enabling users and developers to precisely tailor these models to their specific applications and needs.

Industry observers note that available now in two sizes—1 Billion and 3 Billion parameters—each size comes in both base and instruction-tuned models. Discover the Falcon-Edge series on our dedicated Hugging Face collection.

Recent findings suggest that large Language Models (LLMs), by design, are inherently large and resource-intensive. As demand grows to deploy these models efficiently on edge devices, research into model compression has accelerated. Recent efforts, such as those by DeepSeek and Llama 4, explore training with reduced precision formats—down to FP8—to improve deployment scalability. On the other hand, many state-of-the-art methods emphasize post-training quantization. In contrast to these approaches, BitNet introduces a fundamentally different paradigm: unlike reduced-precision training which still relies on floating-point formats, and post-training quantization which adjusts weights after full-precision training, BitNet operates with the lowest possible precision — ternary weights ({-1, 0, 1}) — directly during training, enabling an end-to-end ultra-efficient model design.

Recent findings suggest that these ternary weights are paving the way for a “matmul-free” LLM design that is notably faster and remarkably memory-efficient in practice. The primary challenge of this innovative approach is the necessity for pre-training BitNet models, which can be computationally demanding and costly for typical users.

Recent findings suggest that leveraging the learnings from pre-training data strategies from our center, we pre-train our model on an internal data mixture for approximately 1.5 Tera Tokens. We use the classic WSD learning rate scheduler for pre-training.

We evaluate our models (base and instruct versions) on the former Hugging Face leaderboard v2 benchmark and report the normalized results below in comparison with other models of similar size:.

Additional results (leaderboard v1) on comparing our instructed models with Microsoft’s upcoming BitNet model:.

Falcon-Edge demonstrates on-par and better performances than models of comparable sizes on the leaderboard v2 tasks, demonstrating that it is possible to train powerful BitNet models on desired domains while being competitive enough on other tasks.

If we look closer at the formula of the BitNet linear layer for inference (in terms of Python code):.

Recent findings suggest that the normalization activation_norm_quant quantizes the activations in int8 format, then the activation is computed back in half precision by diving it by x_scale. Since the model has been trained with fake 8-bit activation quantization, we argue that it is possible to approximate that:.

Therefore, instead of quantizing the model post-training, injecting the weight scale after quantizing the weights should lead to a good enough “approximation” of the non-BitNet version of the model:.

We confirm this by running end-to-end evaluations on the bfloat16 variant of our 1B and 3B base models and below are the results:.

The bfloat16 counterparts of the models can be loaded directly via Hugging Face transformers by passing revision="bfloat16" in the from_pretrained function:.

Recent findings suggest that to the best of our knowledge, except from the most recent release from Microsoft previous BitNet releases only focus on releasing the final quantized model, making it usable only for inference. Similarly to the release from Microsoft, we propose to extend the accessibility of research and application of BitNet models by releasing their pre-quantized weights. That way, people can either perform fine-tuning on their target domain, or do continuous pre-training of the BitNet checkpoint as long as nn.Linear layers are replaced by BitnetLinear layers, and by making sure to quantize the model post training in BitNet format. Since the weights corresponds to the pre-quantized weights, performing text generation without replacing the nn.Linear layers with BitnetLinear layers will produce gibberish output.

The pre-quantized weights can be downloaded via Hugging Face's transformers library by specifying the revision argument to be prequantized:.

This way, we will help fostering an ecosystem around first powerful 1-bit fine-tunes by the community. We provide to community the tools to get easily started and fine-tune their own version of powerful BitNet models by packaging all needed utility methods for performing fine-tuning on the pre-quantized weights on a Python package called onebitllms that we will cover in the next section.

In this release, we also introduce onebitllms - a lightweight Python package that can be plugged into your favorite LLM fine-tuning tools in order to fine-tune any pre-quantized BitNet model. At this time of writing onebitllms exposes these main functionalities:.

At the moment, only full-finetuning is supported through this framework, while in this release the model sizes are relatively small, supporting Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for BitNet models remains an exciting and impactful open question for upcoming BitNet models.

To get started, simply install the package directly through pip or from source, and take a look at examples/ folders inside the source code.

With this package, we hope to accelerate research and development around ternary format LLMs, and hope to see many derivations of Falcon-Edge and other future powerful BitNet models developed by the community.

We believe this release opens up multiple interesting directions - among all the possible follow up directions, we at the moment think that the following open questions will make BitNet models much more impactful in the near future:.

If you find this work useful for your research and work, please consider citing our work, as well as citing all the foundational work behind BitNet models:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xiaomi is pushing the limits of modern smartphone specs with a killer design, flush camera lenses, and a next-gen Snapdragon SoC.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for a phone with top-tier specs, Xiaomi has a upcoming phone for you. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are the company’s latest flagships, available starting today, November 17. When looking at the spec list for the Xiaomi 18 series, it’s difficult to find anything that was left out.

In a recent development, during the launch presentation, Xiaomi emphasized that its newly introduced privacy display wasn’t just a copy of “other privacy displays.” Rather, they created an entirely new subpixel layout called HyperRGB 2.0 that delivers far higher resolution and brightness output than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. You can also enable and disable the privacy display feature on the Xiaomi 18 Pro series with a click of the new AI button on the left side of the phone. Functionally, Xiaomi’s privacy display looks nearly identical to Samsung’s, including the ability to have specific apps use it.

Both models feature identical specs, including the privacy display and cameras, with the exception of the screen size, battery capacity, and charging speed. Here are the differences:.

#57779. Latest Update: AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Massive US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1533 w)

AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Massive US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia.
  • First off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra.
  • In a recent development, but just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia. But who controls the flow of chips also controls the flow of leading frontier AI models. OpenAI reportedly now supports a bipartisan push in the U.S. Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI accelerators and equipment. But are the additional AI safety concerns genuine, or are they also a convenient way to shore up its position at the top of a fast-moving industry? We speak to experts like Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, to find out more.

First off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. The manufacturer debuted the model in September with eye-popping claims that it was the firm’s most capable and best-aligned system yet. OpenAI’s own testing suggested that Astra was much better at following instructions and respecting boundaries. In one internal computer-use safety benchmark, the proportion of misaligned outcomes fell from 18.8% with GPT-5.6 Sol to 3.4% with Astra.

In a recent development, but just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe. OpenAI noted Astra’s written reasoning was harder to monitor than its predecessor’s when they were testing its ability to evade oversight. The model began to recognize when it was being watched and altered its explanations to suit the study, making it harder to tell when it was actually doing something they didn’t want.

It’s a classic problem for AI alignment experts to try and resolve.

It has been revealed that for years, developers have relied on monitoring an AI model's chain of thought — its written working — to understand what it is doing. But if increasingly powerful AI models become better at hiding their reasoning processes, that oversight becomes harder to do.

OpenAI says that Astra still struggles to hide reasoning when it’s carrying out complex tasks, and its evaluation results suggest it has strong overall alignment, but there are worrying signs of a trade-off here.

Sources indicate that those worrying signs become even more so when AI systems are being deployed with more autonomy. In July, OpenAI models ducked its internal evaluation restrictions to gain access to research infrastructure and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, and to IT systems controlled by the Australian and Canadian governments.

Industry observers note that against that backdrop, calls for stronger safety measures seem entirely reasonable. But Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, believes the debate risks overlooking an uncomfortable conflict of interest. "I think a lot of these views about AI safety are very genuinely held," he told Tom’s Hardware Premium in an interview.

But commercial considerations loom large, he reckons. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are spending huge sums developing and deploying models, while facing questions about whether their competitive advantages can survive the arrival of increasingly capable, cheaper alternatives — particularly as they go out and seek funding from the public through an IPO. "They don't have huge moats, even if they’ve acquired a lot of owners,” von Thun stated. “They’re definitely vulnerable.”.

Those vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly obvious. A September report from Mozilla estimated the capability gap between leading closed American models and their open-weight competitors had narrowed to just over four months.

That matters because open-weight models give people the freedom not to rely on a manufacturer’s subscription services. They can be deployed on infrastructure controlled by the customer, modified for specialised tasks, and operated at lower costs. But to the discomfort of U.S. companies, many of them are based in China. And it’s at that point that AI safety gets muddled with geopolitics.

In July, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic, despite their fierce commercial rivalry, had found a common cause: warning U.S. policymakers about the dangers of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Kristy Loke, an AI governance researcher at King's College London who specialises in China's approach to the technology, questions the timing. "It's very suspicious timing asking for pacing," she told Tom's Hardware Premium, referring to calls for slowing frontier AI development just as Chinese open-weight models are undercutting their American rivals on price.

Loke believes companies genuinely worry about the risks. But she also thinks they're worried about their commercial prospects. "they're calling for pacing because they have some safety concerns, they have some commercial anxiety," she said.

Recent findings suggest that she believes some influential people in American AI have increasingly sought to "paint open models in a very bad light", portraying them as inherently less secure than closed alternatives. Yet the risks of AI systems misbehaving aren't restricted to models developed in China, as OpenAI's own incidents demonstrate.

Sources indicate that but open-weight models come with their own risks. Because their underlying parameters can be modified, third parties can create and distribute "abliterated" models, removing the refusal behaviours designed to prevent AI from responding to potentially harmful requests. Many of these models are available on platforms including Hugging Face. “They’re not adding in new behaviour; they’re just removing this refusal behaviour,” said Catherine Flick, professor of ethics and games technology at the University of Staffordshire, in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium. Abliterating models doesn’t make them more capable, Flick said, but it does mean they can answer questions they previously wouldn’t have been willing to. That also means those responses might not have been tested for accuracy or hallucinations.

Those in favour of open-weight models like DeepSeek and Qwen say that removing those guardrails helps security researchers understand how AI behaves. Flick said that’s plausible, but “I just don’t really buy it,” she said. She reckons that the negative potential outputs outweigh the positive case for abliteration because when they’re publicly available, preventing their misuse becomes tricky. American labs clearly have commercial reasons to criticise open-weight competitors because the latter undercuts their economics, but it also doesn’t mean their concerns about safety aren’t valid, too.

Industry observers note that von Thun fears that could result in precisely the wrong kind of regulation. "I think what we should not be doing is allowing the companies to basically form a safety cartel," he said.

Yet U.S. AI companies benefit from the government's determination to maintain its advantage over China. Von Thun argues the Trump administration has created an environment in which economic power translates into political influence, allowing major technology companies to invoke national security concerns when arguing for policies that may also serve their commercial interests. But that could backfire. "I think completely closing off the market to AI products from other countries, including China, would not be the right approach," von Thun noted.

Part of the reason that wouldn’t be the right approach is that the idea that the United States is focused on developing AI responsibly while China isn’t is a fallacy. Just earlier this month, Reuters reported that ByteDance had established a dedicated Alignment & Preparedness team, recruiting researchers to investigate safety risks arising from increasingly capable AI systems.

For von Thun, the solution is to prevent either industry or geopolitical competition from determining what safety means. He points to the European Union's AI Act, which establishes obligations for developers of general-purpose AI models classified as posing systemic risks. The obligations require companies to conduct model evaluations, adversarial testing, cybersecurity measures and also to report serious incidents.

It has been revealed that the opposition to the EU’s AI Act from American tech companies, U.S. politicians and the general public who grouse about the way it delays access to cutting-edge models for Europe’s 450 million citizens demonstrates that these provisions don't automatically solve the alignment problem. But they at least involve more people in the conversation about what is and isn’t acceptable for AI than just the industry's biggest participants.

It has been revealed that even when AI companies agree to independent oversight, they still want some say over how it works — and their own internal decision-making on what is and isn’t safe differs from that of those outside the organization. Loke warns that leading AI companies are experimenting with recursive self-improvement, where models help develop their successors, potentially making it more difficult for humans to understand how decisions are being made. "They’re still attempting more risky methods to train AI that will make the AI harder to control," she remarked.

Von Thun also believes competition rules and interoperability requirements could help prevent AI companies from locking customers into proprietary ecosystems as their agents become increasingly embedded in everyday workflows.

There are plenty of good reasons to be concerned about alignment, particularly when the models being developed are becoming more capable and more difficult to monitor. But letting the companies responsible for building them determine what constitutes an acceptable risk, and who can compete, brings its own dangers. “I’m not saying we don’t need to worry about safety,” said von Thun, “but we should about letting the companies do it.".

What Actually Happens When a Kafka Region Fails?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • In a recent development, most Kafka deployments in the industry initiative to survive the loss of a single Kafka broker or an availability zone.
  • It has been revealed that in such scenarios, the failure model should consider not just the loss of a broker or a zone, but the loss of an entire region.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
