Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here for millions of players who own a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X / S, and those who initiative to buy a console, despite rising costs this year, just to play it. As you have likely already noticed, the launch is inescapable, and that’s especially tough if you’re a PC gamer.

It has been revealed that I’m sorry to remind you that the clock has only just now started ticking down to the unannounced yet inevitable release of the PC version. Good luck with avoiding Twitch and browsing the internet while trying to remain oblivious to the violent (and romantic) delights that await you.

In a recent development, seeing Leonida in true 4K at an unlocked frame rate with full ray-tracing effects and extended draw distances, among other graphical improvements, might be a thing you can do on your PC as early as sometime in Q1 2027, if recent reports are accurate. Regardless, early 2027 is not right now. Speaking as someone with a capable gaming desktop, I’m sad to say that FOMO has already gotten the best of me. I bought GTA VI on the PS5 and will probably double-dip and buy it again on PC, just like I did with GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2. The psychology of me, a weak-willed consumer, is one that publisher Rockstar Games and really any other company in its position would be happy to exploit.

The PC version of GTA VI will launch, eventually, in a very different landscape than the PC ports of Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA V did. Despite the recent downturn in PC sales driven by increased RAM prices, there are considerably more players on PC now than there were a decade ago. SteamDB’s charts show that Steam’s concurrent consumers alone have more than doubled (from around 20 million to over 40 million now) since 2020.

A chunk of those people are likely made up of console expats who decided to migrate to PC for various reasons. Some wanted to experience the fun of building their own desktop, while some were mainly convinced by the fact that you can get more power for your money with a PC than with a PlayStation 5 Pro or Xbox Series X. For a subset of people, the convenience of getting something like a Steam Deck to bring your PC game library with you anywhere more than makes up for its lack of power. There are many other justifiable reasons for making PC your main gaming platform, like getting faster access to discounts on digital games, not paying for online multiplayer, ultrawide monitor resolutions, being able to buy games from one of several platforms, and having one device that you can use for work and play.

Rockstar seems poised to deliver the definitive version of GTA VI on PC on its own terms, and I’m interested to see what the end result will be. In addition to building the best-looking version of the game made to run well across countless configurations, its PC optimization efforts are likely also more focused than before on ensuring decent performance on lower-end hardware (including PC handhelds). With a 200-plus-gigabyte install size on consoles, I dread how substantial it’ll be on PC.

Ideally, the PC version will launch alongside an improved version of GTA Online (whether it’s free to play is anyone’s guess), and maybe with upgraded GTA roleplay tech to support it. I’m hopeful that the PC version of GTA VI will come in early 2027, but if the numerous delays of the console versions were any indication, the developer will take all the time it needs to get it right.

Following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang, there are warnings that vital Nvidia employees are planning to leave if the tech giant doesn’t reinstate him. According to the Wall Street Journal, an employee sent an internal letter to the top executives and board of directors stating that “failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent.’” Huang resigned last week amidst a firestorm of reports about an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a further affair with VP of health care Kimberly Powell, and allegations the former relationship may have facilitated chip smuggling into China.

According to WSJ’s sources, director of developer technology Nader Khalil wrote the letter, urging that Huang be reinstated as CEO, lest the organization lose loyal and important employees. The letter’s recipients, according to WSJ, comprised roughly 60 direct reports and the 10 members of the board, and Khalil warned that “Irreplaceable talent at Nvidia is now contemplating departing.”.

It has been revealed that the internal letter, along with the standwithjensen.com open letter to reinstate him, shows how key Huang is to the employees of Nvidia. Without the key long-term employees, which the company heavily depends on, progress could halt, or possibly regress, as Nvidia would lose the employees who have worked on and built the architectures and systems that make Nvidia what it is, along with their leader, Huang — who has recently stated that he would be honored to come back as CEO.

The open letter, signed by multiple Nvidia current and former employees, and tech CEOs and investors, states that employees are concerned that Huang was ousted unfairly and without due process, expressing that the employees do not have “access to the board’s private deliberations,” and that they have not been shown evidence that Alice Huang was indeed a spy, which even US intelligence doesn’t have solid evidence of. The open letter demands that Huang be reinstated as CEO while ensuring an independent investigation and a fair hearing, including providing a “specific, evidence-based explanation” of why Nvidia shouldn’t keep Huang as CEO — with Huang scheduled to appear before a House of Foreign Affairs panel concerning his affairs with the alleged spy.

In a recent development, despite the letter, the support of other Silicon Valley CEOs, and even President Trump, Nvidia is still not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Nvidia is the hottest AI hardware company at the moment, and its employees are highly desirable not only within the US, but possibly China as well. China surely wouldn’t mind getting its hands on a few key employees, who, if they choose to leave, are likely not going to have a hard time finding another job.

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

Industry observers note that “WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta update, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp people.

#57753. Industry News: 🐯 Liger GRPO meets TRL

📅 25 May 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1255 w)

Industry News: 🐯 Liger GRPO meets TRL

📅 25 May 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality.
  • Fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning.
  • However, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality. We also added support for FSDP and PEFT, making it easier than ever to scale GRPO across multiple GPUs.

Fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning. RL has traditionally been applied to optimize large language models (LLMs) using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. This approach, often associated with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), utilizes a separately trained reward model to guide the fine-tuning of the primary model.

However, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results. The success of RLHF also depends on the capability of the reward model to effectively discriminate between desired and un-desired behaviour from our model.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has seen significant recent popularity alongside DeepSeek's R1 model. GRPO eschews the pre-trained reward model and value models used in RLHF and instead relies on verifiable reward functions which can check the correctness of a model's output in a closed-form manner without needing an external reward model. This has resulted in massive improvements when using GRPO instead of PPO for fine-tuning on domains which are easily verifiable, such as teaching a model to reason, and perform well on math and coding tasks.

The following diagram reveals the GRPO vs PPO training pipeline (ref: Figure 4 of DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models):.

That said, RL training still eats up a ton of GPU memory, so there's still plenty of room for optimizations here. In this blog post, we talk about an optimization that we recently added to TRL that cuts peak memory usage by 40% during GRPO Training, and we also dive into how to scale GRPO to multiple GPUs and nodes without losing performance or correctness.

In a recent development, we extended the Liger Chunked Loss approach to the GRPO Loss, which lets us avoid having to store the full logits in memory for every training step. The calculation of logits, which involves the model's output head, is a significant contributor to peak memory usage, especially when dealing with large vocabularies, long sequence lengths, or large batch sizes. We address this by chunking the input to the lm_head across the batch and running the forward pass one chunk at a time.

But if you just implement it in a straightforward way, you won't actually be able to reduce the peak memory since you'd still need to keep all the logits in GPU memory for the backward pass. To get around that, we calculate the gradients for each loss chunk (with respect to the input chunk and the lm_head weight) during the forward pass, and then accumulate them as we go through each chunk.

Here's the visualization of the optimization (ref: Byron Hsu):.

We recently integrated Liger GRPO with TRL in PR #3184, so now you can use the Liger GRPO loss just by setting use_liger_loss to True in your GRPOConfig and enjoy the memory savings!

Heads up: these features aren't in the latest TRL release yet, so you'll need to install TRL from source for now:.

and then you can use it like this:.

We ran a bunch of GRPO experiments with and without the Liger GRPO Loss to see how things compare. For the policy model, we used Qwen3-0.6B and played around with different batch sizes. All the experiments were run on the gsm8k dataset using its reward functions.

Industry observers note that here's the plots of peak memory usage vs batch size for both FP32 and BF16 training. As expected, the memory savings get better with larger batch sizes since we chunk along the batch dimension. So when the batch size goes up, the Liger chunked loss ends up using a lot less memory, up to 40% less, compared to the regular (non-liger) version.

Sources indicate that quick note: Right now, we only support FP32, but we're working on open-sourcing BF16 support for Liger GRPO in TRL. The BF16 results shown here are from internal patches we've been testing.

We also show that Liger Loss is effectively accurate. As seen in the plot, rewards over training steps stay pretty much the same as what you'd see using the standard TRL implementation.

In a recent development, we also added FSDP and PEFT support to Liger GRPO Loss in PR #3260 and PR #3355, respectively, allowing users to easily scale their experiments across multiple GPUs or nodes. PEFT techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA reduce the number of trainable parameters by only tuning the weights of smaller adapter weights on top of the original model, significantly lowering memory pressure as gradients, activations, and optimizer states for the entire model don't need to be held in memory. Additionally, using PEFT in GRPO allows one to forgo loading a separate reference model during training, as we can obtain the original, unmodified model during training by simply disabling the LoRA adapters.

Here, we show a multi-GPU GRPO training plot using FSDP and PEFT, where we compare the maximum training batch size possible with and without the Liger Loss across different Qwen3 model sizes. We found that with Liger, we were able to bump up the batch size by around 1.5 to 1.8x!

To accelerate text generation during training, Liger Loss can be effectively combined with TRL's integrated vLLM server. This significantly speeds up the collection of rollout data with minimal overhead and offers a seamless integration experience.

Sources indicate that start the vLLM Server: First, launch the vLLM server. This server will handle the generation requests from your training script. Open a terminal and run:.

Note: We assign CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 to run the vLLM server on a specific GPU (GPU 1 in this case), leaving other GPUs free for training.

Industry observers note that configure and Run Your Training Script: Next, modify your training script to use the vLLM server. The key change is setting use_vllm=True in your GRPOConfig.

Sources indicate that launch the Training: Finally, run your training script using accelerate launch (or python if not using Accelerate for multi-GPU/distributed training). Make sure to target a different GPU for training if your vLLM server is occupying one.

(Assuming your script is named train.py and you want to run training on GPU 0).

By following these steps, you can leverage vLLM for faster generation turnarounds during your GRPO training with Liger Loss.

Sources indicate that with the integration of Liger-GRPO into TRL, alongside FSDP and PEFT support, fine-tuning language models with GRPO is now more memory-efficient and scalable than ever. We encourage the community to try out these latest features and share their feedback to help us further improve RL training for LLMs.

Does Liger Kernel affect training speed at all? Is it faster, slower, or no difference compared to regular GRPO?
